headline: One-eighty on the sounder: haddock steady on the mud, cod thin on the gravel, bluefin working the Basin
subhead: Warm water has the cod grounds quiet, but the mackerel schools pulling bluefin over Stellwagen Basin are the best sign we've had all month.
body_markdown:
One-eighty feet on the sounder, mud from rail to rail, and the haddock have been sitting on it like they're bolted down. That's the number I keep coming back to this week — 180 to 210 feet on the Stellwagen mud, southeast of the Basin toward the edge of Tillies. Clean marks stacked two to four feet off bottom, and when the boat's holding right on the drift, guys are doubling up on haddock in the 3 to 5 pound class, some pushing 7. High-low rigs, size 6/0 hooks, fresh clam or a chunk of squid — nothing fancy needed. The haddock don't care about finesse this time of year, they care about you being on the mud and staying there.

Cod is the harder conversation. Warm water's pushed the surface layer down deep enough that the gravel edges — the classic 120 to 150 foot stuff off the northwest corner of the Bank and along the edge toward Carter Canyon — have gone quiet in the middle of the day. We're still picking cod, don't get me wrong, but it's a early-morning and evening game right now, and the fish have slid a little deeper and tighter to structure than they were in June. Diamond jigs and Norwegian-style jigs tipped with a strip of squid are outfishing bait on the drift — the jigging motion seems to wake fish up that are just sitting heavy on bottom in this warm-water stretch. If you're anchoring bait, go heavier on the sinker than you think you need; the current's been running harder than usual off the moon, and a slack presentation just sits there doing nothing.

Pollock have been a bonus fish more than a target — scattered marks up off bottom on the high spots around Stellwagen Edge and the northern end of Tillies, taking the same jigs meant for cod on the drop. Hake we're still finding at night on the deep mud in the Basin, 250 feet plus, for the guys willing to run out after dark with a chum bag and clam bait. Not glamorous fishing but it's steady if you know where the mud holds bait.

Now for the part of the report I actually want to talk about. The bluefin have shown up over Stellwagen Basin and along the edge toward Cape Cod Tails, and they're doing it the way they're supposed to in August — chasing mackerel balls that the whales are working right alongside them. If you see fin whales or humpbacks up on the surface out there this week, slow down and look around before you run past — nine times out of ten there's mackerel underneath them, and where there's mackerel stacked that thick, the bluefin aren't far. We've had fish show on top chopping bait, 50 to 80 pound class mostly, with a few bigger ones mixed in that nobody's landed yet. Live mackerel on a stinger rig has been the most consistent producer when you can jig a few up and keep them lively in the tank. Butterfly-style jigs worked fast through the school when the fish are down and not showing on top have also drawn strikes, but it's been a game of patience — you can sit on a good-looking whale push for twenty minutes and get nothing, then have it go off in a five-minute window.

Honest read on the tuna: it's not an every-day fish yet. Three trips out to the Basin and the Tails this week, we had shots on two of them, and only boated fish on one. That's not bad for early-to-mid August on the Bank, but it means you need to be willing to run around a little and read the birds and whales rather than parking on a number and hoping. The mackerel schools have been thick enough on the sounder — big red blobs from 30 to 60 feet down — that I don't think this bite is going anywhere for a while, but it moves around with the bait, and the bait moves around with the tide and wind.

Wind's been out of the southwest most afternoons, building a light chop by early afternoon that's made the morning bite the better window for everything — groundfish and tuna both. If you're planning a trip, I'd be leaving the dock in the dark and trying to be on the mud or working bait pushes by first light, because by 1 or 2 in the afternoon the wind picks up enough to make jigging sloppy and the tuna schools tend to scatter deeper.

Looking ahead, I expect the haddock bite on the mud to hold steady through the next week — that fishery doesn't care much about surface temperature, it's a bottom game and the bottom's been consistent. Cod should improve some as we get into cooler overnight temps and the water column starts to mix a little more, but I wouldn't call it a sure thing yet — I'd fish the early morning tide change on the gravel edges and not expect much midday. For the bluefin, if the mackerel stay stacked over the Basin and the whales keep working there, this could turn into the best stretch of the summer for shots at fish. If that bait pushes off the Bank the way it sometimes does late in August, I'd shift attention toward Tillies and the deeper edge toward the canyon approaches. Either way, keep an eye on the birds and the whales before you even wet a line — out here, they'll tell you where to fish before your fishfinder does.
